phase1.intro:
Every primitive type has a matching wrapper class — int pairs with Integer, double with Double, and so on.

What do you want to look at first?

topics.buttonText: Why do wrapper classes exist at all?
dialogue: [[key:The wrapper is a real object, while the primitive is just a raw value]] — and that distinction is exactly why wrappers exist at all.

stickyNote.flavor: 📦 a real object standing in for a raw value
stickyNote.definition: Every primitive has a matching wrapper class (int↔Integer, double↔Double). The wrapper is a real object; the primitive is a raw value.

dialogue: [[term:Autoboxing]] is Java automatically converting a primitive into its wrapper for you — `Integer intObj = 42;` looks like assigning an int to an Integer, but Java quietly wraps it behind the scenes.
[[term:Unboxing]] goes the other direction, automatically pulling the primitive back out of a wrapper when you need it.

stickyNote.flavor: 🔄 Java quietly wraps and unwraps for you
stickyNote.definition: Autoboxing automatically converts a primitive into its wrapper object. Unboxing automatically converts the wrapper back into a primitive.

topics.buttonText: Why would I want the object version, and what's the trap?
dialogue: [[key:Three real reasons]]: collections like `ArrayList` can only hold objects, wrappers can be `null` (a primitive never can), and wrappers bundle utility methods like `Integer.parseInt("123")`.
[[warn:But that null possibility is also the trap]]: unboxing a `null` wrapper throws a `NullPointerException`, since Java has no way to represent "null" as a raw int.

stickyNote.flavor: ⚠️ collections and nullability, but null unboxes to a crash
stickyNote.definition: Wrappers enable collections of primitives and a real null state, plus utility methods. Unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException.

phase1.openingDialogue: Wrapper classes let primitives act like objects — autoboxed and unboxed automatically, but null is a real trap when unboxing. 📦

phase2.errorMessage:
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "java.lang.Integer.intValue()" because the return value of "..." is null
        at Test.main(Test.java:6)
phase2.explanation:
[[warn:Unboxing a null wrapper is exactly what crashes here]]. `x` is declared as `Integer` and explicitly set to `null` — perfectly legal, since wrappers CAN be null. But the moment `int y = x;` tries to unbox it back down to a raw `int`, Java has to call a method on `x` behind the scenes to pull the value out, and [[warn:calling any method on a null reference throws a NullPointerException]].

[[key:The fix is always checking for null before unboxing]]: `if (x != null) { int y = x; }`. This exact gotcha — a wrapper silently holding null right up until the moment you unbox it — is one of the most common sources of unexpected crashes in real Java code, especially once wrappers start passing through several layers of methods.

mcq.question:
What happens when you unbox a wrapper object that's currently null (e.g. int y = someNullInteger;)?

A) y is automatically set to 0
B) A NullPointerException is thrown
C) It's a compile error
D) y stays null too

phase4.selfChallenge:
Write a program that:
1. Uses autoboxing to create Integer, Double, Boolean objects
2. Uses parseInt() to convert "999" to int
3. Uses Integer.MAX_VALUE and Integer.MIN_VALUE
4. Creates an ArrayList<Integer> and adds 5 numbers using autoboxing
5. Prints all numbers using unboxing

phase5.trivia: [[fun:Fun fact]]: Java secretly caches and reuses Integer objects for small values, from -128 to 127, which is why `Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; a == b` can actually come back true, while the exact same comparison with 200 instead of 100 comes back false. It's a real, well-known gotcha — and exactly why you should always use .equals() to compare wrapper objects, never ==, regardless of what the numbers happen to be.
phase5.openingDialogue: One more thing before you go wrap things up~
